justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It points to the unguarded `isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)` call on a non-number handle that may be null or undefined, which throws a TypeError during scheduling. It notes the old code guarded against this case. That is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: In `patchTimer`'s `scheduleTask`, the change stores the native timer's return value in `handleOrId`. When it is not a number, it executes `data.isRefreshable = isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)`. Some environments return null or undefined from `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`requestAnimationFrame`, for example a browser extension, policy or automation wrapper that blocks the call. The old code explicitly tolerated a nullish handle. With this change, reading `.refresh` on null throws a TypeError synchronously, so calling the patched `setTimeout` crashes instead of returning. The fix uses optional chaining (`handleOrId?.refresh`) so a nullish handle is treated as non-refreshable.

For those environments the new code throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'refresh')` while scheduling, which is a regression.

justification: The known bug is newline content being dropped by `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/` because `.` does not match newlines, now that parts with newlines inside parentheses are no longer split. Finding [0] describes a different defect: `slice(prefix.length, -1)` mishandles pseudo-function parts that carry a suffix after the closing paren (e.g. "`:is(.a):hover` becomes `:is(.a):hove)`"). It does not mention newlines or the regex `.` behavior.
ground_truth: In `ShadowCss._scopeSelector`/`_applySelectorScope`, the change replaced the simple `/ ?, ?/` comma split and the combinator separator with regexes that do not split inside parentheses. A selector part like `.foo:is(.a,\n.b)` therefore now reaches `_scopeSelectorPart` as a single string that can contain newlines. That function splits the part with `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/`, both in the newly added pseudo-function `:host` branch (`scopedP.match(...)`) and in the non-host branch (`t.match(...)`). Because `.` does not match a newline, everything after the first newline is silently dropped. For example, a component style `.foo:is(.a,\n.b) {}` is emitted as `.foo[contenta]:is(.a,`, with the rest of the selector and the closing parenthesis lost, which breaks the stylesheet. The fix changed the trailing group of both regexes to `([\s\S]*)` so content after newlines is kept.

findings.description: The pseudo-function handling assumes any selector part starting with `:where(` or `:is(` ends with the matching `)`, and drops the last character with `slice(prefix.length, -1)`. Parts like `:is(.a):hover`, `:where(.x).active` or `:is(.a, .b).foo` have a suffix after the closing paren. The final character of the suffix gets chopped, and the remaining `)` and suffix are then scoped as if they were inner selector content. The generated CSS is corrupted, for example `:is(.a):hover` becomes `:is(.a):hove)`. The `:where(a):where(b)` test only passes because of this same quirk.

findings.description: The code assumes any part that starts with `:where(` or `:is(` also ends with the matching `)`, and unwraps it with `selectorPart.slice(prefix.length, -1)`. justification: Finding 0 matches part of the known bug. It says the afterRenderEffect "calls `init()` on every update," so each run adds another `highlightComponent` listener and "recreates both InjectorTreeVisualizer instances." That is the core mechanism of the bug: D3 runs layout inside a display:none element, and it would lead a maintainer to the fix. Finding 1 is about unused sortedProviders, which is unrelated.
ground_truth: This change rewrites `InjectorTreeComponent` to render from an `afterRenderEffect` that runs whenever the `componentExplorerView` input changes. The change also hides the deferred `ng-injector-tree` with `[hidden]` (display:none) and removes the old `ng-injector- tree.hidden` CSS, which had kept the element laid out with `visibility: hidden`. So once the Injector Tree tab has been opened and the user switches to another tab, every new component explorer view re-runs the effect. D3 then tries to lay out, translate and snap SVG trees inside an element with no layout, which throws errors. `init()` also runs on every effect execution, re-registering the `highlightComponent` listener and recreating the visualizers each time. The fix adds a `hidden` input bound to the host's `[hidden]`, returns early from the effect when it is true (read untracked), and calls `init()` only once, when the visualizers do not exist yet.

findings.description: The afterRenderEffect reads `componentExplorerView()` and calls `init()` on every update. Each run also recreates both InjectorTreeVisualizer instances, which resets zoom, pan and the rendered graph on every forest update. Previously the listeners and setup ran once, in `afterNextRender`.

The template still passes the raw `providers()` input to `ng-injector-providers`. The new `sortedProviders` computed is never used. Providers were previously sorted by token before display, so the list now appears unsorted, which is a regression.

Visibility is now toggled with the `[hidden]` attribute on component host elements instead of a `display: none` class. The native `hidden` attribute is overridden by any author CSS `display` rule, such as a `:host { display: block/flex }` rule on these components. Inactive tabs may therefore stay visible and overlap. The old `ng-injector-tree.hidden` workaround (visibility hidden, absolutely positioned) was also removed, so a hidden injector tree may be laid out with zero size for the d3 visualizer.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the unconditional `get_fields_from_path` call for `__` names. It notes that this call raises an uncaught `FieldDoesNotExist` when the path ends in a property or method (e.g. `parent__some_property`), crashing where the value previously rendered. That is the same defect as the known bug. Finding 1 describes a different issue: a ForeignKey final field being misused in `items_for_result`.
ground_truth: The change makes `lookup_field()` in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py` call `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` unconditionally whenever a `list_display` name contains `__`, so it can render boolean icons for related BooleanFields. Before this, such names were resolved only by walking attributes with `getattr`, which also works for paths whose last part is not a concrete model field, such as a method, a property or `__str__` on a related model. `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` for those paths, and the exception is not caught. Because `lookup_field` is shared by the changelist and readonly-field rendering, entries traversing relations, including second-degree ones (e.g. `book__author__get_full_name` or `parent__parent__some_property`), now crash with an exception where they previously displayed fine. The fix removes this lookup from `lookup_field`. It instead resolves the final field only in `items_for_result` when `f` is None, wrapped in `try/except FieldDoesNotExist`.

findings.description: `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)` is called whenever the name contains `__`, but the preceding loop also accepts non-field attributes on related objects, such as a property or method result like `parent__some_property`. For those, `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` or `NotRelationField`. Neither is caught, so the changelist crashes where it previously rendered the value. The same happens for a name like `parent__is_active__foo`.

`f` is now the related model's final field, but `items_for_result` still treats it as a field of the row object. If the final field is a ForeignKey (for example `parent__parent`), the code runs `getattr(result, f.name)` on the wrong model. This raises `AttributeError` or shows the wrong value, instead of using the traversed value. Fields with choices or other formatting also go through `display_for_field` with a value taken from a different path. This changes behavior beyond boolean icons.

justification: The known bug has two parts. Finding [0] identifies the BooleanField part with the same mechanism: "forms.BooleanField.to_python turns any string other than 'false', '0' or 'False' into True, so it never raises ValidationError. A search for 'foo' on `bool__exact` therefore becomes `bool=True` and matches every True row." It does not mention the choices/TypedChoiceField case, but it pinpoints the same faulty validation code and one of the described failure mechanisms. That would lead a maintainer to the actual bug.
ground_truth: The change rewrote `ModelAdmin.get_search_results` so that, for non-text `__exact` search fields, each search term is validated with `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`. Lookups whose term raises `ValidationError` are skipped; all others are passed to the ORM with the converted value. This validation does not reject invalid terms for two kinds of fields. First, fields with `choices` produce a `TypedChoiceField`, whose `to_python()` returns the raw string unchanged. So searching "john" against an `IntegerField(choices=...)` with `field__exact` sends "john" to the ORM, which raises `ValueError` and makes the changelist return HTTP 500. Second, `forms.BooleanField.to_python()` maps almost any non-false string to True, so an arbitrary term like "xyz" against `bool__exact` matches every row where the field is True instead of matching nothing. The fix uses `formfield.clean()` for Typed(Multiple)ChoiceField so values are coerced and validated, and uses strict boolean and null-boolean parsers that raise `ValidationError` for unrecognized strings.

justification:
Finding 0 describes the same defect: "a line that is only "
" or empty wraps to [] and is dropped" and "Text ending in "

ground_truth:
The rewritten `django.utils.text.wrap()` loops over `text.splitlines(True)`, passes each line to `textwrap.TextWrapper.wrap()`, and joins the pieces with "
". `TextWrapper.wrap()` returns an empty list for an empty or whitespace-only line, so those lines vanish from the output. With the default `replace_whitespace=True`, the trailing newline kept by `splitlines(True)` becomes a space and is dropped, so a trailing newline in the input is lost too. For example, `wordwrap("first

second
", 80)` returns "first
second" instead of "first

second

".

justification: Finding [0] matches the known bug. It says the check `".. " in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals, because for constants `.var` is the resolved string rather than a Variable. It notes the warning wrongly fires for `{{ "a..b" }}` and that valid templates would fail once the check becomes an error. Its suggested fix is to apply the check only to variable lookups, which is the same mechanism and fix as the known bug. Finding [1] raises a different issue: `origin` could be None.
ground_truth: The new deprecation check in `Parser.parse()` for variable nodes tests `".." in str(filter_expression.var)`. For constant expressions, `filter_expression.var` is the resolved literal value (a string or translated string), not a `Variable` lookup. So a template containing a literal with two consecutive dots, such as `{{ "a..b" }}` or `{{ 'a..b'|upper }}`, wrongly emits a `RemovedInDjango70Warning` about double-dot lookups. That warning becomes an exception when warnings are treated as errors. The check would also reject valid templates once it is elevated to an error as planned. The fix applies the check only when the expression is a variable lookup: `filter_expression.is_var and ".." in filter_expression.var.var`.

findings.description: The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals. For a constant such as `{{ "Loading..." }}` or `{{ "a..b" }}`, FilterExpression sets `.var` to the resolved string rather than a Variable. The deprecation warning then fires for a valid literal that has no double-dot lookup. Under the planned error elevation, valid templates would fail to compile. The check should apply only when `.var` is a `Variable` that is a lookup, not a literal.

The warning message reads `self.origin.name`, but `Parser.origin` defaults to None when a Parser is built without an origin. Parsing a variable containing `..` would then raise AttributeError instead of emitting a warning.

It also proposes restricting the check to Variable lookups, which matches the actual fix.

findings.description: The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches string literals. For a constant such as `{{ "Loading..." }}` or `{{ _("Wait..") }}`, FilterExpression resolves `.var` to the plain string content. justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says the ColPairs built with `queryset.model._meta.db_table` instead of resolving the field through the query "breaks when the target fields live on a parent table (multi-table inheritance), because the columns are qualified with the child's table". It also notes that the old `field__in` path resolved the field correctly. That is the known bug's mechanism. Finding 1 is about the removed single-column optimization, performance, and None handling, which is a different issue.
ground_truth: `ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.get_prefetch_querysets()` now filters with `TupleIn(ColPairs(queryset.model._meta.db_table, related_fields, related_fields, self.field), ...)`, where `related_fields = self.field.foreign_related_fields`. Those are fields of the FK's target model, but the table alias comes from the prefetch queryset's model. With a custom prefetch queryset on a multi-table- inheritance subclass of the target, the two do not match. Example: a FK to `Place` prefetched with `Prefetch("place", queryset=Restaurant.objects.all())`. The generated SQL references the parent's column (e.g. `id`) on the child's table, which has no such column, so `prefetch_related` crashes with a database error. The old `field__in` kwarg filter resolved the field names through the ORM and did not have this problem. The fix resolves each field by name against the prefetch queryset (`queryset.query.resolve_ref(field.name).target`), so the columns match the queryset's model.

findings.description: The prefetch filter now builds ColPairs with `queryset.model._meta.db_table` as the alias, instead of resolving the field through the query. The generated SQL therefore always references the model's own table by name. This breaks when the target fields live on a parent table (multi-table inheritance), because the columns are qualified with the child's table. It also breaks when the base table alias differs from the table name, for example a custom prefetch queryset that was already aliased. The result is a wrong-column or missing-table error, or wrong rows. The old `field__in` path resolved the field correctly through the ORM.

The join-less single-column `field__in` optimization is removed, so every ordinary single-column FK prefetch now goes through the composite-key `TupleIn` path. This produces a row-value style `(col) IN ((v1),(v2))` clause. Some backends handle that poorly, and it can hurt index usage or hit parameter limits. Null FK values such as `(None,)` are also now passed raw into the tuple lookup, where the old code relied on the `In` lookup to strip them. This is a regression risk for the most common prefetch case.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says passing `writer="html"` as a string fails on docutils versions before 0.22, which expect a Writer instance: "the string is treated as the writer object ... fails with an AttributeError". It also notes this breaks all admindocs RST rendering, which matches the known bug.
ground_truth: In `django/contrib/admindocs/utils.py`, `parse_rst()` was changed to call `docutils.core.publish_parts(..., writer="html", ...)` instead of `writer_name="html"`, to silence a deprecation warning in docutils 0.22+. Passing a string writer name through the `writer` parameter only works in docutils 0.22+. In docutils 0.19–0.21, `writer` must be a writer instance. With an older docutils installed, every admindocs reStructuredText rendering (docstrings for views, models, template tags, filters) therefore fails, typically with an AttributeError when docutils treats the string "html" as a writer object. The fix creates an instance with `docutils.writers.get_writer_class("html")()` and passes that as `writer`, which works across docutils 0.19 through 0.22.

findings.description: `writer="html"` replaces `writer_name="html"`. Before docutils 0.22, `publish_parts` expects `writer` to be a Writer instance and takes names only through `writer_name`. With an older docutils, the string is treated as the writer object and `Publisher.set_components` skips the name lookup because `writer` is not None. `parse_rst` then fails with an AttributeError such as `'str' object has no attribute 'write'` or `'translate'`. This breaks every admindocs page that renders RST (views, models, template tags and filters) for users on docutils versions that Django still supports.

justification: The only finding, [0], is about the tooltip spans losing their `title` and getting `aria-label`, which is an accessibility concern. The known bug is that the new `<button>` elements have no `type="button"`. They therefore default to submit and hijack implicit form submission when a user presses Enter. Finding [0] does not address this.
ground_truth: In `SelectFilter.init` in SelectFilter2.js, the change replaced the "Choose all", "Choose selected", "Remove selected" and "Remove all" `<a>` links with `<button>` elements built via `quickElement('button', ...)`. None of them is given a `type` attribute. Inside a form, a button with no type defaults to `type="submit"`. When a user presses Enter in a text input of an admin change form containing a filter_horizontal/filter_vertical widget, the browser's implicit submission activates the first submit button in tree order. If one of these selector buttons comes first, its click handler fires (moving options, with the event default prevented) instead of the form being saved. The fix adds `'type', 'button'` to all four buttons so they no longer act as submit buttons.

findings.description: The help tooltip spans lose their `title` attribute and get `aria-label` instead. A `span` has no role, so `aria-label` on it is generally ignored by assistive technology. Sighted users no longer get the hover tooltip, so the explanation of the filter input is no longer reliably exposed to anyone. The same applies to the selected-filter span.

justification: Finding [0] identifies the same defect. It says the check "uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields", which causes a false "nonexistent field '-name'" E012 error. It also notes that the old code used `fields_orders`, which matches the known bug and its fix exactly. Findings [1] and [2] describe different issues: the W037/W040/W043 generator logic, and checks being skipped or duplicated per database.
ground_truth: The new `Index.check()` method passes `{*self.fields, *self.include, *references}` to `model._check_local_fields()`. `self.fields` holds the raw field strings, including the "-" prefix used for descending order. The old Model-level check used the field names from `index.fields_orders`, which has that prefix stripped. As a result, a valid index such as `models.Index(fields=["-name"], name="idx")` now fails the system check with "'indexes' refers to the nonexistent field '-name'" (models.E012). The fix passes `field for field, _ in self.fields_orders` instead of `self.fields`.

findings.description: The field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields (e.g. `fields=['-name']`). `_check_local_fields` therefore reports a false 'refers to the nonexistent field "-name"' error (models.E012) for valid descending indexes. The old code used `fields_orders`, which strips the prefix. Building a set also makes the order of reported errors nondeterministic.

W037 checks `any(self.condition is not None for index in model._meta.indexes)`, so the generator ignores `index` and tests `self.condition`. If the current index has a condition, the warning is emitted for all indexes. If another index on the model has a condition but this one doesn't, no warning is emitted for that other index's own turn... it is only emitted when it is itself checked, which is fine, but the expression is plainly wrong. The W040 and W043 checks have a related fault: they scan every index on the model from inside a per-index method, so a model with N indexes gets the same warning N times, and indexes that don't use the feature still trigger it.

All index checks now run only inside the `for db in databases` loop and are skipped when no database is routable or `databases` is empty/None. Name checks (E033/E034) and field-reference checks (E012 etc.) are no longer run in those cases, which is a regression. With multiple databases, every error is duplicated once per database. The tests had to be changed to pass `databases=self.databases` to keep passing.

Finding 1 is about the checks being moved inside the per-database loop, and finding 2 is about duplicate feature warnings. Both describe different issues.

Since `check` is now called once per index, a model with several indexes gets duplicate warnings, and an index without `include` or expressions gets a warning meant for another index. Each check should look only at `self`.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It says `window.relatedWindows` is undefined in production because the IIFE-local `relatedWindows` is never assigned to `window`, so "`window.relatedWindows.indexOf(win)` would throw a TypeError. `win.close()` would never run, and the popup would stay open." It also notes that the test's `beforeEach` hides the problem by initializing the array itself. This is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: In `RelatedObjectLookups.js`, the change rewrote `dismissRelatedLookupPopup` to use `window.relatedWindows.indexOf(win)` and `window.relatedWindows.splice(index, 1)` instead of the IIFE-local `relatedWindows` array. The module never assigns `relatedWindows` to `window`, so in a real admin page `window.relatedWindows` is undefined. Calling `.indexOf` on it throws a TypeError before `win.close()` runs. As a result, picking an object in a raw-id/related lookup popup sets the value but leaves the popup open. The new test hid the bug because it created `window.relatedWindows` itself. The fix went back to the module- local `relatedWindows`, exported it as `window.relatedWindows = relatedWindows`, and removed the test's own initialization.

findings.description: The code now reads `window.relatedWindows`, but in this file `relatedWindows` is, as far as I recall, a block-scoped `const` inside the IIFE-style block, and nothing in the diff shows it being assigned to `window`. In production, `window.relatedWindows` would be `undefined`, so `window.relatedWindows.indexOf(win)` would throw a TypeError. `win.close()` would never run, and the popup would stay open after the user selects an object. The new test hides this because its `beforeEach` sets `window.relatedWindows = []` itself, so it does not exercise the real code path. The other places that push to or splice `relatedWindows` still use the local variable, so they would be inconsistent with this change.

justification: Finding 0 is about duplicate appending of `db_returning` fields when the value is an expression (`returning_fields.append(field)` running unconditionally). The known bug is different. It is about the `elif field.db_returning: returning_fields.remove(field)` branch, which drops `db_returning` fields that have explicit non-expression values, leaving stale in-memory values even on RETURNING-capable backends. The finding never mentions that removal.
ground_truth: In the insert branch of `Model._save_table`, the change builds `returning_fields = list(meta.db_returning_fields)` and then, for each insert field, calls `returning_fields.remove(field)` (the `elif field.db_returning:` branch) whenever the field's pre_save value is not an expression. Before this change, every `db_returning` field was always fetched back via RETURNING and assigned to the instance. Now a `db_returning` field with an explicitly set value keeps the in-memory Python value instead of the value the database actually stored. This happens even on backends that support RETURNING (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle). For example, an explicitly set primary key or a custom `db_returning=True` field whose stored or converted value (via `from_db_value`, normalization or triggers) differs from the assigned value is left stale on the instance after `save()`/`create()`. The fix only removes such fields from `returning_fields` when the backend cannot return columns from insert, and never removes the auto field when the pk was set.

findings.description: In the insert path, `returning_fields.append(field)` runs unconditionally whenever the value has `resolve_expression`. A field with `db_returning=True` (for example a `db_default` field left unset, whose value is a `DatabaseDefault` expression, or one assigned an expression) is already in `meta.db_returning_fields`. It is therefore appended a second time, so the same column appears twice in the RETURNING clause. This can break the INSERT on backends that reject duplicate returning columns. It also makes `_assign_returned_values` set the attribute twice, and it can misalign values with fields. The fix is to append only if `field not in returning_fields`.

justification: The known bug is that `returning_fields.remove(field)` drops explicitly set `db_returning` fields even on RETURNING-capable backends, so the instance keeps a stale in-memory value instead of the database-stored one. Finding 0 is about duplicate appends of an expression field, which is a different issue. Finding 1 targets the same removal branch, but its failure mechanism is different. It describes MySQL/MariaDB, where removing the auto field causes `last_insert_id` to be zipped into the wrong expression field. It also recommends restricting removal to backends that *can* return columns, which is the opposite of the actual fix. Under that recommendation, the stale-value problem on RETURNING backends would persist. So it does not identify the known defect.

findings.description: In the insert path, if a field with db_returning=True (already in meta.db_returning_fields) is assigned an expression, it is appended to returning_fields a second time. The RETURNING clause then contains the column twice, and the field's value is assigned twice from duplicate returned values. The append needs a `field not in returning_fields` guard.

The `elif field.db_returning: returning_fields.remove(field)` branch runs on every backend. On backends without can_return_columns_from_insert (MySQL/MariaDB), if the pk is explicitly set and another field is assigned an expression, the auto field is removed from returning_fields but the expression field is appended. The compiler's non-RETURNING path then returns last_insert_id as a single value, and _assign_returned_values zips it with the first returning field. That puts the lastrowid into the expression field instead of deferring it, so the field gets a wrong value. The removal must be restricted to backends that can return columns and must skip the auto field when the pk is set.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says the function "now raises ValueError for over-long codes, but callers that pass untrusted input only catch LookupError". It names the cookie path and the URL path prefix through get_language_from_request and get_language_from_path, and says the result is an uncaught ValueError producing a 500 in LocaleMiddleware. This matches the known bug's mechanism.
ground_truth: The security patch added a length check to `get_supported_language_variant()`. When `lang_code` exceeds `LANGUAGE_CODE_MAX_LENGTH` (500) and no generic variant can be cut off (or `strict=True`), it raises `ValueError("'lang_code' exceeds the maximum accepted length")`. This breaks the function's documented contract of raising `LookupError` when nothing is found. Callers like `LocaleMiddleware` and `get_language_from_path()`/`get_language_from_request()` only catch `LookupError`, and with the default strict=False a long code without a usable "-" still reaches the `ValueError` branch. So a request whose URL language prefix or language cookie is longer than 500 characters crashes with an unhandled ValueError (HTTP 500) instead of falling back to another language. Fixed by raising `LookupError(lang_code)` instead of ValueError.

A request with a cookie over 500 characters, or a path like /xxxx.../, that has no '-' before the limit (or a strict lookup) raises an uncaught ValueError. LocaleMiddleware then returns a 500 error, a regression for requests that used to fall back to the default language.

A request path like /xxxx…(>500 chars)/ now raises an unhandled ValueError, which produces a 500 error instead of a normal 404 or fallback. This is a regression of existing behavior.

justification: The known bug is that `db_type` includes length/precision parameters (e.g. varchar(50)), so the explicit cast silently truncates or rounds values. Finding 0 flags `db_type` vs `cast_db_type` only because serial pseudo-types cause a syntax error, which is a different failure mechanism. Finding 1 is about discarded custom placeholders and None or non-castable types. Neither finding mentions silent truncation or rounding caused by parameterized types.
ground_truth: The new `SQLInsertCompiler.assemble_as_sql` in the PostgreSQL compiler builds each UNNEST placeholder as `(%s)::<db_type>[]`, where `db_type` comes from `field.db_type(self.connection)`. That type string includes the column's parameters, e.g. `varchar(50)` or `numeric(5, 2)`. In PostgreSQL an explicit cast to a length- limited type silently truncates or rounds values instead of raising an error. So `bulk_create()` of two or more objects whose CharField value exceeds `max_length` silently inserts a truncated string, where the regular VALUES insert would fail with a "value too long" error. The same applies to rounding of decimals. The fix strips the parameters from the type (`db_type.split("(")[0]`), so the cast is to e.g. `varchar[]` and the column's own constraints apply on insert.

findings.description: The cast type is built from `field.db_type()` rather than a cast-safe type (`cast_db_type`). For AutoField, BigAutoField and SmallAutoField, `db_type` is `serial`, `bigserial` or `smallserial`. These are pseudo-types and cannot be used in a cast, so `(%s)::serial[]` is a PostgreSQL syntax error. Any `bulk_create` of 2 or more objects with explicit primary keys on an auto field will now crash. That path is common, for example when pks are supplied or a fixture is loaded. The `endswith('[]')` check does not catch this case.

The UNNEST path discards per-field placeholders (`field.get_placeholder`) and any other field-specific SQL wrapping. It builds the casts purely from `db_type`. Fields that rely on custom placeholders, such as geometry fields or custom fields, will be inserted incorrectly or fail. Fields whose `db_type` is None or non-castable are also not excluded.

It says nothing about silent truncation or rounding through length-limited casts. Finding [1] is about GIS and custom placeholders being ignored, which is unrelated. Neither finding identifies the truncation mechanism.

justification: The known bug is a pickling failure caused by the mismatch between the namedtuple's type name ("Attachment") and its module-level binding (`EmailAttachment`). ground_truth: The change adds the module-level `EmailAttachment = namedtuple("Attachment", ["filename", "content", "mimetype"])` in `django/core/mail/message.py`. `EmailMessage.attach()` now stores each attachment as an instance of it. No `Attachment` attribute exists in `django.core.mail.message`; the class is bound to the name `EmailAttachment`. The fix renames the namedtuple type names to match their variable names (`namedtuple("EmailAttachment", ...)`, and likewise `EmailAlternative`).

justification: The known bug is that `_ipv6_address_from_str` calls `len()` on non-string inputs (e.g. IPv6Address instances, ints), which raises an uncaught TypeError in `is_valid_ipv6_address`. ground_truth: The change makes `is_valid_ipv6_address()` call the new helper `_ipv6_address_from_str()` instead of `ipaddress.IPv6Address(ip_str)`. justification: Finding 0 identifies the faulty guard: it checks `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` instead of the cache for `select.id`. This is the same mechanism as the known bug: add_to_cache is called on a select that SelectBox does not manage, causing a TypeError. ground_truth: The change added a block to `updateRelatedSelectsOptions` in RelatedObjectLookups.js that, after appending a new option to another related select, calls `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, option)` and `SelectBox.redisplay(select.id)`. The guard is only `window.SelectBox !== undefined && !SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]`; it never checks that `select` itself is managed by SelectBox. Consider a form with several relations to the same model where only some use `filter_horizontal`, so SelectBox.js is loaded. Adding an object via the '+' popup then reaches other plain `<select>` widgets that have no `SelectBox.cache` entry. `add_to_cache` then pushes onto an undefined cache entry and throws a TypeError. That aborts `dismissAddRelatedObjectPopup`, so the popup window never closes. The fix adds the condition `SelectBox.cache[select.id]`, so the cache is updated only for fields SelectBox actually manages.

justification: Finding 0 describes the exact mechanism: the `%d` interpolation is applied before `ngettext`, so the msgids never match the catalog and the error always appears in English. ground_truth: The new `MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message()` applies `% self.min_length` to each string literal before passing it to `ngettext`. The msgids that `ngettext` receives are therefore already formatted strings, such as "This password is too short. It must contain at least 8 characters.". These never match the translation catalog entries, which contain the `%d` placeholder. As a result, with a non-English active language (e.g. French), the too-short password error is always shown untranslated in English. The fix calls `ngettext` with the unformatted singular/plural msgids and applies `% self.min_length` to the translated result. It also restores `params={"min_length": ...}` on the raised `ValidationError`.

findings.description: The `%d` interpolation is applied to the msgid strings before they reach `ngettext` (`"...%d character." % self.min_length`). The lookup keys become e.g. "...at least 8 character.", which don't exist in any translation catalog. The original msgids with `%(min_length)d` therefore never match, and the too-short error is always shown in English, even for locales that have translations. It also generates a different msgid for every `min_length`, and makemessages would no longer extract the original strings. The interpolation should be done on the result of `ngettext`.

justification: Finding 3 states that `Permission.objects` is used without `.using(db)`, so when migrating a non-default database the queries hit the router's default database instead of `schema_editor.connection.alias`. Findings 0, 1 and 2 describe different issues: duplicate signal handlers, substring matching on the model name, and custom permission codenames being rewritten.
ground_truth: In the new `RenamePermission._rename`, the code reads `db = schema_editor.connection.alias` but never applies it to the lookups. `ContentType.objects.filter(...)` and `Permission.objects.filter(content_type_id__in=...)` therefore run against the default (router-chosen) database rather than the one being migrated. Running `migrate --database=other` on an app with a `RenameModel` reads and renames permissions in the default database, or finds nothing there. Meanwhile the permissions in the database actually being migrated keep their old codenames and names. The fix adds `.using(db)` to both the ContentType and Permission querysets so the operation works on the migration's database connection.

findings.description: `pre_migrate.connect` is called without a `sender`. `emit_pre_migrate_signal` fires once per app config with the same `plan`, so `rename_permissions` runs once per installed app. Each run inserts another `RenamePermission` after every `RenameModel`, leaving N duplicate operations. The duplicates are wasteful and redo the rename. The `assertOperationsInjected` test only checks the next operation, so it would not catch this. The handler should be connected with `sender=self`.

The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, a substring match. Renaming `Foo` also selects content types and permissions of unrelated models such as `foobar` or `myfoo` in the same app. Those permissions are then renamed to `*_<newmodel>`, which corrupts them. It should be an exact match on `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the content type is rewritten using `codename.split('_')[0]` as the prefix and a generated name. Custom permissions such as `can_export_oldmodel` or `publish_article` become `can_newmodel` or `publish_newmodel`, losing their meaning. Several custom permissions can also collapse to the same codename. The code never checks that a codename actually has the `<action>_<oldmodel>` form, and the generated name replaces any custom permission names.

When migrating a non-default database, the live Permission model reads and writes the router's default database instead of `schema_editor.connection.alias`. justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It notes that the new MRO scan "collects every property found in any class's __dict__ and never checks whether a more-derived class shadows that name with a non-property." It identifies the same consequences (Model.__init__ kwargs handling and the get_or_create/update_or_create checks) and proposes the same fix of tracking names already seen.
ground_truth: The rewritten `Options._property_names` iterates over `self.model.__mro__` and adds every name whose value in some `klass.__dict__` is a `property`. It does not check whether a class earlier in the MRO already shadows that name with a non-property attribute. Example: an abstract parent model defines `foo` as a `@property` and a child model overrides `foo` with a plain attribute or a field. `foo` is still reported in the child's `_property_names`. Code that relies on this set then treats the name as a property and mishandles it, for example `Model.__init__`/`_prepare_related_fields` kwargs handling and `QuerySet` create/update_or_create validation. The old `inspect.getattr_static` version resolved the attribute as normal lookup would. The fix tracks names already seen in earlier MRO classes and only counts a property if its name was not defined in a more-derived class.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the exact defect: "`self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field` compares Field instances. ground_truth: The new `Subquery.resolve_expression()` is meant to drop the Subquery shim and return the bare resolved `Query`. It is supposed to wrap the query in an `ExpressionWrapper` only when the user passed an `output_field` that differs from the query's own. It tests this with `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field`, but `Field.__eq__` compares fields by `creation_counter` and model, not by kind. So a separately instantiated field such as `IntegerField()` never equals the query's model field. As a result, any `Subquery(..., output_field=X())` is always wrapped in an `ExpressionWrapper`, even when `X` is the same field type as the selected column. Lookups that introspect the right-hand side as a `Query` then no longer recognize it, defeating the purpose of the change. One example is the tuple lookups' `isinstance(self.rhs, Query)` check, which is supposed to raise `NotSupportedError` for composite-pk comparisons against subqueries. The fix compares field types (`type(self.output_field) is not type(resolved.query.output_field)`) instead of using field equality.

findings.description: resolve_expression reads `self.output_field` and only catches AttributeError. When the subquery's output field cannot be determined (for example a values() query with several columns, or a queryset with no single select column), BaseExpression.output_field raises FieldError, not AttributeError. The error would now surface eagerly at resolve time instead of lazily, and the intended fallback of returning `resolved.query` would be skipped. Previously working subqueries, such as multi-column `__in` subqueries, could crash.
